newsitem.title: UK: Protestant parade pride in N.Irish-British links.
newsitem.headline: Protestant parade pride in N.Irish-British links.

text.p: Bonfires blazed across Northern Ireland on Saturday ushering in Protestant festivities marking a victory that still riles Catholic Irish after 300 years.

Tens of thousands in the staunchly pro-British Orange Order backed by blaring brass, flute and bagpipe bands, bring the province to a standstill each "Twelfth of July" in processions that touch a raw nerve among the Catholic minority.
Wearing traditional regalia of orange shoulder-sashes and London-style bowler hats, their chief officers strut city highways and country lanes bearing silver swords and pikes.
Massive silken banners swaying in the light summer breeze are emblazoned with Christian biblical scenes and images of Protestant King William defeating Catholic King James in 1690.
They parade a pride in Protestantism and three centuries of British sovereignty in a province where the 40 percent nationalist population want an all-Ireland state freed of British influence.

Scarred by guerrilla war by pro-Irish and pro-British militias, the region has been on a tightrope of fear ahead of Saturday's climax of a Protestant "marching season" that always revives simmering sectarianism.
Late on Thursday, in what was widely hailed as a momentous decision, the Order tilted the province away from the prospect of open conflict and tried to build a new peace.
The Order called off plans for four parades that had sparked threats of mass mobilisation by nationalists.
All sides in the beleaguered region had feared confrontations would erupt in communal blood-letting.

It was an about-turn that took everyone by surprise. It won the Order plaudits from Protestant and Catholic groups but also provoked rumblings of discontent from Orange Order factions who said that rebellious Catholics were being appeased.
Five people were injured when security forces came under fire in Belfast on Friday night in a grim reminder that Northern Ireland's troubles were far from over, despite the Orange gesture.

Relations between the Catholics and Britain's Labour government nose-dived last Sunday when a massive police and military operation was launched to ensure the Orange Order could hold its most controversial parade, which went through a Catholic neighbourhood of the town of Portadown.
Catholics accused London of betraying their hopes that the "Orangemen" would not be prevented from going through their zone.
Last year the Northern Ireland police blocked Orangemen for four days but reversed their decision in the face of an eruption of Protestant violence across the province.
Last Sunday the chief of police said that the march had to go ahead because he feared pro-British "loyalist" extremists would otherwise have killed Catholics.

Northern Ireland's Orangemen proclaim themselves as "true born Britons" and their mottos of "not an inch" and "no surrender" are timeless testimony to a determination not to be dragooned into a "United Ireland".
Catholics living in enclaves say swaggering Orange parades and the noisy drums and bands fill them with apprehension.
The Orangemen, whose organisation is strong in rural Northern Ireland and has countless "lodges" or branches in towns and cities, insist that they mean no offence.
They regard the ability "to walk the queen's highway" as an inalienable right won by forefrathers who defeated Catholic King James and helped secure a Protestant monarchy in Britain.
Catholics retort that the Order's attitudes have been frozen for 300 years but they say the calling-off of four marches on Friday is a welcome sign of a thaw.
